extracted.intended_audience: General readers and students of Montaigne / readers of classical essays and moral philosophy
extracted.subtask_description: Close reading and application of Montaigne's moral and stylistic precepts as expressed in his Essays (on retirement, solitude, writing, and conduct). Useful for literary study or adopting his practical maxims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be one's own / self-governance
rubrics_metrics.description: “The greatest thing in the world is for a man to know that he is his own.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Break the knot of obligations; make leisure to disentangle yourself from external importunities; aim to keep the remainder of life for yourself without being so bound that removal would 'flay us' — govern yourself with reverence to reason and conscience and be ashamed to make a false step before them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Withdraw when you can no longer add to society
rubrics_metrics.description: “’Tis time to wean ourselves from society when we can no longer add anything to it; he who is not in a condition to lend must forbid himself to borrow.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Retire from public life when your active contribution wanes; do not remain out of vanity for glory or reputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare retirement by reasoned moderation
rubrics_metrics.description: One ought to model a new retired life 'by the rules of reason, and to institute and establish it by premeditation and reflection.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before retiring, shake off passions and obligations, take leave of labour, and set up a measured plan of life suited to your humour and capacities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose agreeable, non-laborious employments in retirement
rubrics_metrics.description: “The employment a man should choose for such a life ought neither to be a laborious nor an unpleasing one; otherwise ’tis to no purpose at all to be retired.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select activities that preserve health and cheerfulness; keep enough engagement to avoid the 'dull and stupid laziness' of total idleness without over-committing to burdensome tasks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use externals but do not base contentment on them
rubrics_metrics.description: “We are to use these accidental and extraneous commodities, so far as they are pleasant to us, but by no means to lay our principal foundation there; ’tis no true one; neither nature nor reason allows it so to be.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enjoy material conveniences in moderation; do not enslave your contentment to the power of another or to transitory fortunes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid excessive asceticism that harms health
rubrics_metrics.description: Extremes of self-denial (throwing away wealth, extreme mortifications) are 'acts of an excessive virtue' and can be hurtful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moderate religious or philosophical austerities; do not sacrifice bodily health or practical comforts for ostensible virtue when such excesses are injurious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate anticipatory imagination of misfortune
rubrics_metrics.description: Practice representing to yourself, as far as imagination can stretch, the ill to come (death, poverty, sickness) to lessen fear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use mental exercises (as at jousts and tiltings) to counterfeit war in peace; this prepares you to face misfortunes with equanimity and borrow from examples of those who endure with patience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject ambition and public glory in solitude
rubrics_metrics.description: “Ambition is of all others the most contrary humour to solitude; glory and repose are things that cannot possibly inhabit in one and the same place.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you truly retire, relinquish concern for fame and public approbation; otherwise your retreat is only a prelude to re-entering public life for applause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be honest and avoid falsification in writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Montaigne refuses 'to forge vain names to direct my letters to' and is 'a sworn enemy to all manner of falsification.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write genuinely (address real friends rather than invented recipients); avoid artificiality and false pretenses when composing letters or essays.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer substance over ornamental eloquence
rubrics_metrics.description: “Away with that eloquence that enchants us with itself, and not with actual things!”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticizes eloquence that dazzles but lacks substantive matter; writing should instruct or show action ('not to speak, but to do well') rather than merely display stylistic virtuosity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write only what you know — no more
rubrics_metrics.description: “Write what he knows, and as much as he knows, but no more.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid overreaching or pretending knowledge; favor modest, truthful communication and avoid puffed-up claims intended for reputation rather than truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Favor plain, familiar, and candid style over ceremonious flattery
rubrics_metrics.description: Montaigne confesses a 'humorous and familiar style' and states 'I mortally hate all air of flattery,' explaining his blunt, rough manner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shun excessive ceremonious formalities and flattery in letters and speech; be candid, even if it appears crude, because genuine feeling should be readable in the heart rather than manufactured in words.
